text:
B: Hi! Hello, can you hear me? Sorry, I think I was on mute for a second.
A: Yes, yes, I can hear you. Hello. How are you?
B: I'm good, thank you, a bit shattered, but good. I'm Marta. And you're Gurpreet?
A: Yeah, Gurpreet. Nice to meet you. You had busy day?
B: Erm, sort of, yeah. I'm a pharmacist at a hospital, on the cardiology wards, so it's lots of checking drug charts and talking to patients before they go home, you know, explaining their blood thinners and things. And the Victoria line this morning was absolutely rammed, I had someone's elbow in my face the whole way. What about you, what do you do?
A: Er, I work in factory near Heathrow. Food packaging. I run the tray-sealing line, for ready meals, sandwiches, like that.
B: Oh, so the sandwiches people buy at the airport?
A: Yeah, yeah, some of them going to airport, some supermarket. I'm part-time now, three shifts in a week.
B: That sounds quite nice, actually, part-time. Is that your choice?
A: Er, yeah, sort of. I hurt my back two years ago, so the physio said little bit less. It's okay now. Little bit hard sometimes, but okay.
B: Oh, I'm sorry. Backs are horrible, honestly. We see so many people on the ward who've been, you know, lifting things for thirty years. Do you do exercises for it?
A: I walk. Lake Farm, near my place, in Hayes. I do slow lap, every day off. That's it, really.
B: That's lovely. I swim, or I try to, twice a week before work, but the pool in Leyton is always freezing, so sometimes I kind of stand at the edge and think about it and then go home.
A: Ha. Cold water, no, I can't.
B: And what do you do on the weekends, apart from walking?
A: Sunday I go gurdwara in Southall, mostly. And I'm growing chillies and coriander in pots, on the patio. This year chillies are doing really well, I don't know why.
B: No way! I'm growing tomatoes in our tiny garden and they've finally, finally gone red. I was so excited I sent a photo to my mum in Poland.
A: Ah, you're from Poland? Nice.
B: Yeah, from Gdańsk, but I've been here fifteen years now, so I'm kind of half and half. What chillies are they?
A: Er, green ones, the small hot ones, like we use in India. My partner Simran says too many now, we have to give to neighbours.
B: That's the best problem to have. Is Simran into the gardening too?
A: Not so much. She's teaching assistant, primary school, so she's tired after work, the kids, you know. She likes eating the chillies, not growing.
B: Ha, yeah, no, totally. My husband's the same with my tomatoes, he just appears when they're ready. He's a teacher as well, actually, geography. He spends the whole weekend marking at the kitchen table, and our cat sits on the paper.
A: You have cat?
B: We do, Pierogi. He's a tabby and he's, erm, a bit round. He knocks everything off the worktop, one thing a day, like it's his job.
A: Pierogi, like the food?
B: Exactly like the food! Polish dumplings. He looks like one, honestly. Sorry, I'm talking so much. How did you find the puzzle at the start?
A: Er, it was okay. Last one was hard, I took long time. I think maybe I got it.
B: Better than me, I gave up on the last one and just stared at it.
A: That's okay, no problem. Everybody is like that, innit, with puzzles. Like my cousin, he—
